fact: The sprinklers-to-dripline guide the City of Longmont publishes says to remove the sprinkler heads a new drip layout doesn't need and cap the pipes, leaving them in the ground.
quote: Cap Unnecessary Sprinkler Heads: Remove sprinkler heads that are not needed for the new drip line layout and cap the pipes - leaving them in the ground. This prevents leaks and pressure loss in the system but helps you avoid digging them all out of the ground.
source_label: City of Longmont, Sprinklers to Dripline Irrigation: How to Transition Your Irrigation from Sprinklers to Dripline (prepared by ClimateScaping, posted December 2025)
notes: Written for lawn-to-xeriscape conversions (planted beds, where a leak shows), not for turf. The City links it from its Conserving Water Outdoors page as 'Sprinklers to Dripline Irrigation'; the PDF's own header is ClimateScaping's. Upload path dates it to 2025-12.

fact: The Longmont-published guide converts a zone by fitting a conversion kit to one central sprinkler head and says each zone turned into drip needs a backflow device and a pressure reducer added in the valve box first.
quote: Convert Needed Sprinkler Heads to Dripline: Choose a central sprinkler head in each zone to serve as a connection point for the dripline going to your trees and plants. Replace this head with a conversion kit, which will allow you to attach drip tubing directly to the existing underground line. Note: When you convert a sprinkler zone to a drip line zone, you need to add a backflow device and pressure reducer to that line in the ground manifold box first. You must do this to each zone being used for drip line to trees or plants.
source_label: City of Longmont, Sprinklers to Dripline Irrigation: How to Transition Your Irrigation from Sprinklers to Dripline (prepared by ClimateScaping, posted December 2025)
notes: CSU Extension 4.702 puts the backflow device ahead of the control valve and the filter and pressure regulator after it; the page says 'the guide Longmont publishes' and pairs it with CSU's equipment order.

fact: The Longmont-published guide says to set drip zones to run less often but longer, typically 15 to 30 minutes depending on the plants.
quote: Adjust Watering Times: Set your timer to run less frequently but for longer periods. Drip systems are designed to water deeply, so adjust your schedule to ensure moisture reaches deep into the soil (typically running for 15-30 minutes depending on the plants)
source_label: City of Longmont, Sprinklers to Dripline Irrigation: How to Transition Your Irrigation from Sprinklers to Dripline (prepared by ClimateScaping, posted December 2025)
notes: The PDF sentence ends 'plants)l.' (a typo); the quote stops before it.

fact: The Longmont-published guide says tree drip lines must be on their own irrigation zone, not shared with perennials and shrubs.
quote: IMPORTANT: You must set up these tree drip line systems on their own irrigation zone. Your trees should not be irrigated on the same zone as your perennial flowers and shrubs. Tree irrigation zones run for much more time than your perennial garden needs.
source_label: City of Longmont, Sprinklers to Dripline Irrigation: How to Transition Your Irrigation from Sprinklers to Dripline (prepared by ClimateScaping, posted December 2025)
notes: Tree watering itself belongs to the watering-trees-with-artificial-turf guide; this page only links to it.

fact: The Longmont-published guide says the irrigation system should be blown out and shut down before the first fall frost so freezing water doesn't crack the lines.
quote: at the end of the season and prior to the first frost in the fall, the irrigation system should be blown out and shut down for the winter to prevent water freezing and cracking the lines.
source_label: City of Longmont, Sprinklers to Dripline Irrigation: How to Transition Your Irrigation from Sprinklers to Dripline (prepared by ClimateScaping, posted December 2025)

fact: The City of Longmont points residents to a free irrigation assessment from Resource Central (Slow the Flow) that comes with a customized watering schedule.
quote: Not sure where to start? Get a FREE Irrigation Assessment from Resource Central. You’ll receive a customized watering schedule based on your yard and irrigation system.
source_label: City of Longmont, Conserving Water Outdoors
notes: The same page lists 'Irrigation Assessments: Optimize your sprinkler system and get a customized watering schedule with Slow the Flow.' Resource Central's own sprinklers page (resourcecentral.org/sprinklers/) returns 403 to curl.

fact: CSU Extension says a sprinkler head can be converted to feed drip with a kit, but the other heads on that zone must be capped because sprinklers and drip cannot share a zone.
quote: It can even be a high-pressure sprinkler head using a kit to convert it to drip. Keep in mind that other heads in that zone must be capped because sprinklers and drip cannot be mixed within the same zone.
source_label: CSU Extension, Drip Irrigation for Home Gardens, Fact Sheet 4.702 (reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension lists a permanent drip zone's parts in order as backflow preventer, control valve, filter and pressure regulator, because household pressure runs 50 to 60 psi while drip is built for about 20 to 30 psi.
quote: In permanent systems, the order of equipment is backflow prevention device, control valve, filter then pressure regulator. … Typical household water pressure is 50 to 60 psi while drip systems are designed to operate at around 20 to 30 psi depending on the manufacturer.
source_label: CSU Extension, Drip Irrigation for Home Gardens, Fact Sheet 4.702 (reviewed August 2025)
notes: The same sheet: 'Common setup mistakes include not installing a filter or pressure reducer, use of overly long lengths of mainline, and adding too many drip emitters.'

fact: CSU Extension says a sprinkler system should be blown out with compressed air rather than trusted to drain valves, at no more than 80 psi for rigid PVC and 50 psi for flexible polyethylene pipe.
quote: Do not trust manual or automatic drain valves. The system should be blown out with pressurized air. … Ideal pressures are in the range of 40 to 80 pounds per square inch (psi) for the air compressor, with 80 psi being the maximum for rigid PVC pipe and 50 psi for polyethylene pipe (flexible black pipe).
source_label: CSU Extension, Home Sprinkler Systems: Preparing Your Sprinkler System for Winter, Fact Sheet 4.719 (reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says to blow out each zone twice in short cycles, then leave it alone, because air in dry pipe builds heat.
quote: Each zone/station should be blown out twice to make sure all the water is purged from the system. It is better to use two short cycles per station/zone than to have one long cycle. Once a zone is “blown out”, avoid blowing that zone out again. Compressed air moving through dry pipes causes friction and heat which could cause damage.
source_label: CSU Extension, Home Sprinkler Systems: Preparing Your Sprinkler System for Winter, Fact Sheet 4.719 (reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension says an irrigation system on domestic water must have a backflow preventer, and that a pressure vacuum breaker (PVB) or reduced-pressure (RP) device must never be blown out with compressed air.
quote: If your irrigation system is attached to domestic water, it is required to have a backflow prevention device. … Pressure Vacuum Breaker (PVB) or Reduced Pressure (RP) backflow prevention devices must never be blown out with compressed air. The rubber seals inside can easily melt from the heat of the air.
source_label: CSU Extension, Home Sprinkler Systems: Preparing Your Sprinkler System for Winter, Fact Sheet 4.719 (reviewed August 2025)
notes: The sheet has the compressor connect to the blowout fitting downstream of the backflow device, with its downstream ball valve closed.

fact: The Colorado Geological Survey says collapsible soils can lose 10 to 15 percent of their volume when wetted, and names watering and unrepaired leaking water lines among the human causes.
quote: When they become wet, they are subject to rapid collapse and can be reduced in volume as much as 10 to 15 percent. … Human activities are definitely the cause of most soils collapsing. These activities include watering grass and shrubs, failing to repair leaking water lines in utility trenches, impounding water, blocking drainages by highways, loading excessive weight upon collapsible soils, and any activity which increases subsurface moisture in soils prone to collapse.
source_label: Colorado Geological Survey, Collapsible Soils
notes: The CGS page is statewide and does not map Northern Colorado lots; pair with cgs-expansive-soil (clay swells when wet). Never say a given yard has collapsible soil.

fact: A synthetic-turf distributor's installer guidance says the valve feeding a removed lawn must be capped or terminated so no water enters its lines after installation, ideally by removing the valve or capping its outlet line.
quote: If the natural grass is to be removed, then the grass valve must be capped and/or terminated to prevent any water entering the lines after the installation. … It would be smart to remove the valve entirely or cap the valve’s “exit line”.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Irrigation (installer blog)
notes: Trade source (a turf distributor writing for installers), not an agency. Present as 'a turf distributor's guidance for installers'.

fact: The same installer guidance warns that cutting a valve's wires stops it only until someone rewires it.
quote: I have witnessed installers cutting valve wires thinking by cutting them will terminate the valve from turning back on. This is true but remember, it only takes a minute to rewire that valve back up.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Irrigation (installer blog)

fact: The same installer guidance advises against capping heads under turf: shallow pipe can be hit by a nail or staple, and threaded caps may leak over time, eroding the soil and leaving depressions in the turf.
quote: If the pipes are not deep enough, you will chance hitting them with a nail or staple… why put that pressure on your team? … Capping sprinkler heads with threaded caps may leak over time, eroding the soil, and causing depressions in the turf surface.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Irrigation (installer blog)

fact: EPA WaterSense says to check an in-ground irrigation system each spring for frost damage, and that a 1/32-inch leak can waste about 6,300 gallons a month.
quote: If you have an in-ground irrigation system, check it each spring before use to make sure it wasn’t damaged by frost or freezing. An irrigation system that has a leak 1/32nd of an inch in diameter (about the thickness of a dime) can waste about 6,300 gallons of water per month.
source_label: U.S. EPA WaterSense, Fix a Leak Week

fact: Fort Collins-Loveland Water District and Resource Central offer the district's residential and non-residential customers a free 75-minute sprinkler evaluation (Slow the Flow) with tune-up recommendations and a customized watering schedule.
quote: Fort Collins – Loveland Water District and Resource Central can help with a FREE sprinkler evaluation. A 75-minute evaluation could help you save thousands of gallons of water each year. Resource Central associates run efficiency tests on your sprinkler system, make tune-up recommendations to reduce water waste, and provide a customized watering schedule designed to optimize your water use.
source_label: Fort Collins-Loveland Water District, Slow the Flow
notes: FCLWD serves parts of Fort Collins, Loveland, Timnath and Windsor (fclwd-service-area); eligibility is checked on Resource Central's site.

fact: Fort Collins-Loveland Water District gives a $100 bill credit for a WaterSense-labeled smart sprinkler controller bought in 2026, with the receipt emailed by November 30, 2026.
quote: Purchase an EPA WaterSense-certified smart sprinkler controller, rain sensor or rotary sprinkler nozzles (high-efficiency nozzles) in 2026, before 11/30/2026. … EPA Water Sense Certified Smart Controller – $100 bill credit
source_label: Fort Collins-Loveland Water District, WaterSense Smart Sprinkler Rebate Program
notes: Also $25 for a rain sensor and up to $4 per rotary nozzle; one controller and one rain sensor per account per calendar year. The 2026 window closes 2026-11-30.

fact: Fort Collins-Loveland Water District says the pressure vacuum breaker (PVB) is the most common residential backflow device and recommends that single-family homes have their irrigation systems tested every three years, under the state's Regulation 11.39.
quote: The State of Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment requires the FCLWD to adhere to regulations set forth in Regulation 11.39 (Backflow Prevention and Cross Connection Rule). … The most common residential backflow device is a PVB, or Pressure Vacuum Breaker. We recommend that customers in single-family homes have their irrigation systems tested every three years by a certified backflow prevention assembly tester.
source_label: Fort Collins-Loveland Water District, Backflow Prevention

fact: The Town of Windsor says homeowner testing of residential sprinkler backflow devices is voluntary at this time, while businesses served by Town water must test yearly.
quote: The Town of Windsor requires all business and industries serviced by Town of Windsor Water to have their backflow devices tested by a certified tester and results are sent to them annually. This requirement includes, but is not limited to backflow devices on service mains, fire suppression systems, process lines, and sprinkler supply lines. Homeowner testing of residential sprinkler supply line backflow devices is on a voluntary basis at this time.
source_label: Town of Windsor, Backflow & Cross Connection Program

fact: Windsor's water FAQ says a new sprinkler system needs a Town permit, and that repairing, expanding or modifying a system with an unapproved backflow device means upgrading the device, testing it on installation and yearly after.
quote: Yes. The Municipal Code requires that you have a permit before installing a new sprinkler system. … If work is done to repair, expand or modify an existing sprinkler system with an unapproved back flow device, the customer must upgrade the existing back flow device to current standards. The new back flow prevention device must be tested upon installation and then annually by a state-certified tester.
source_label: Town of Windsor, Public Works – Water FAQs
notes: The FAQ is undated and sits beside the backflow program page's 'voluntary basis at this time' for homeowner testing; the page hedges ('It depends … ask Windsor') rather than reconciling them.

fact: Windsor's water FAQ names blowing out a sprinkler system in the fall as one way to raise pressure on the customer's side and push water backward, which is what a backflow preventer stops.
quote: Back pressure is also reversal of water flow in the water system. However, this type of reversal happens when water pressure increases on the customer's side of the water system. Examples of things that can cause pressure increases in your sprinkler system would be injection fertilizing or blowing out the system in the fall.
source_label: Town of Windsor, Public Works – Water FAQs

fact: Colorado's drinking water rule on backflow (Regulation 11.39) says that when a water supplier learns a single-family home's connection is a cross-connection, the supplier decides what backflow protection controls it.
quote: If the supplier becomes aware of a single-family-residential connection to the public water system that is a cross-connection, the supplier must determine the type of backflow prevention assembly or backflow prevention method to control the cross-connection.
source_label: 5 CCR 1002-11.39, Backflow Prevention and Cross-Connection Control Rule (Colorado Regulation 11.39, text via Cornell LII)
notes: Read on Cornell LII's copy of the Code of Colorado Regulations; the Secretary of State's CCR viewer did not return the rule to curl. Rule 11.39(2)(c)(ii).

fact: Colorado 811 does not mark private utility lines such as a home's sprinkler lines; the property owner has them located by a private locating company.
quote: There may be private utilities within your dig area such as sprinkler lines, gas lines, or a BBQ, that require you to higher a private locating company in addition to calling 811. Private Utilities are lines on your property not owned by a public utility company. It is your responsibility to have private utilities marked before digging. Colorado 811 does not mark private utility lines.
source_label: Colorado 811, Residential Property: Planning to Dig on Your Property?
